  module, in **snake_case** — an `Energy` ADE defining `SolarPanel` and `Thermostat`
  both in an `Energy` module share `energy.parquet`, distinguished by `object_type`.
- An extension class that **specialises an existing module's class** (declares no
  module of its own, but subclasses a core or extension type) routes to *that* class's
  module file — an ADE class specialising `Building` lands in `building.parquet`,
  exactly as `BuildingPart` does. This holds recursively.
- **Whether a class carries CityJSON's `+` marker is irrelevant to routing.** An ADE
  class with **no** `+` and a resolvable declared module is a perfectly valid extension
  class, and routes by that module like any other — the `+` is a detail of CityJSON's
  own encoding of extension types, not a precondition for being one.
- A class with **no resolvable `ModuleKey`** at all — not a recognised core CityGML
  class, and not declared as belonging to any extension module, `+`-marked or not — is
  a **hard error**. Routing is total: every class the writer encounters must resolve to
  some file, or the input is rejected.

**No `+` in file names.** CityJSON writes an Extension's object types with a leading `+`
(`+Thermostat`). That marker belongs to CityJSON's encoding, not to the CM, and a `+`
has no business in a file name — so CityParquet strips it before computing the
snake_case file name, while the `ModuleKey` computation above still runs against the
original, un-stripped source type so a module-less extension's identity isn't lost
before it's resolved.

🟡 Carrying full ADE namespace / object-class metadata beyond the `ModuleKey` +
`city.extensions` mapping (below) remains an [open question](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/open-questions).

## Extended semantic surfaces

An extended semantic surface type keeps its source name **inside** the
[`geometry_properties_lod*` JSON value](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/geometry-semantics), including
CityJSON's `+` prefix where the source used one. Semantic surfaces are never promoted
to column names, so there is nothing a Parquet column name would have to reject, and no
renaming is needed.

## Extended attributes

An extended attribute becomes a typed attribute column like any other, so it gets the
same predicate and projection pushdown as a core attribute. CityJSON writes these with
a leading `+` (`+height`). Parquet itself imposes no restriction on a leading `+` in a
column name, but such a name is hostile to SQL and to many query engines (it cannot be
referenced unquoted, and reads as an operator). So for portability the `+` **MUST** be
replaced with `ex_`: `+height` → `ex_height`.

This accepts a low, bounded risk of collision with a genuine `ex_`-prefixed attribute.
The extended attribute columns are listed in the `attributes`
[metadata key](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/metadata) like any other attribute; distinguishing
extension attributes from core ones beyond the `ex_` prefix (and carrying ADE
namespaces) is an [open question](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/open-questions).

## The extension declaration

`city.extensions` ([metadata key](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/metadata)) carries two things per
extension, so export can restore exactly what import stripped:

- The **real Extension/ADE declaration**, as JSON, verbatim from the source (a CityJSON
  Extension's schema document, or the ADE identity CityGML declares) — not
  CityParquet's own summary of it.
- A **`source-name ↔ class ↔ module` mapping**: for each extension class, its source
  spelling (with `+` where CityJSON used one), the `object_type` it was stored under,
  and the `ModuleKey` it was routed by. Export consults this mapping to restore the
  CityJSON `+` on the classes that originally carried it — the `+` is not re-derived
  from `object_type` alone, since a module-routed ADE class may have carried no `+` in
  the first place (see above).

**Open item**

Representing CityGML ADE namespaces and object-class metadata beyond the `ModuleKey` +
this mapping is unresolved — see [Open questions](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/open-questions).

chapters.title: Mapping from CityGML / CityJSON
chapters.description: The reference mapping from CityGML and CityJSON / CityJSONSeq into CityParquet.
chapters.body:
This page is the converter reference: how a source model's fields land in the
CityParquet object table, sidecars, and metadata. It is *informative* — the normative
rules live in the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification) body — but every row here points at
the section that governs it.

## CityGML

CityGML features map to CityParquet object rows directly, since CityParquet encodes the
CityGML conceptual model:

| CityGML | CityParquet |
|---|---|
| feature id | `id` |
| feature class | `object_type` — the CityGML class name verbatim |
| feature hierarchy | `parents` / `children` / `feature_id` |
| feature attributes | inferred typed [attribute columns](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/object-table-schema) |
| geometry, per LoD | [WKB `geometry_lod*`](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/geometry-semantics) |
| boundary surfaces and their attributes | `geometry_properties_lod*` (`surfaces` + `face_semantics`) |
| appearance (surface data) | [`material_lod*` / `texture_lod*`](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/appearance-templates) + sidecars |
| implicit geometry | `template` struct + `geometry_templates.parquet` |
| address | the [`address` column](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/object-table-schema) |
| `CityObjectGroup` + its members | the group is a row (in `generics.parquet`); membership is carried by `children` / `children_roles` / `parents` — no dedicated file |
| ADE feature types / attributes | [extension rules](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/extensions) |

3DCityDB's normalised relational schema is **not** reproduced: its property,
appearance, surface-data and implicit-geometry tables become nullable object-table
columns plus sidecar files (rationale: the
[schema-strategy decisions](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/design-decisions/schema-strategy)). The one place
CityParquet borrows 3DCityDB's shape deliberately is the
[`address` struct](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/object-table-schema), whose fields follow its
`ADDRESS` table.

## CityJSON / CityJSONSeq

| CityJSON field                            | CityParquet mapping                                         |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `CityObjects.{id}`                        | `id`                                                        |
| `CityObjects.{id}.type`                   | `object_type` — mapped to the CityGML class name (`TransportSquare`→`Square`, `GenericCityObject`→`GenericOccupiedSpace`, `BuildingStorey`→`Storey`, `TunnelHollowSpace`→`HollowSpace`; others unchanged; any `+` stripped) |
| `attributes`                              | inferred typed [attribute columns](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/object-table-schema) |
| `children` / `parents` / `children_roles` | same-named columns                                          |
| `address`                                 | the [`address` column](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/object-table-schema); `address[].location` becomes a WKB `MultiPointZ` |
| `geometry[].boundaries`                   | encoded into [WKB `geometry_lod*`](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/geometry-semantics) |
| `geometry[].lod`                          | the column's LoD suffix (`lod2_2`); exact source spelling not separately retained |
| `geometry[].semantics`                    | `geometry_properties_lod*` — `surfaces` verbatim, `values` flattened to `face_semantics` |
| `geometry[]` shell nesting                | `geometry_properties_lod*.shells`                           |
| `geometry[].material`                     | [`material_lod*`](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/appearance-templates) for the geometry's LoD |
| `geometry[].texture`                      | `texture_lod*` for the geometry's LoD                       |
| `geometry[].template`                     | `template.id`                                               |
| `geometry[].transformationMatrix`         | `template.transformationMatrix`                             |
| geometry instance reference point         | `template.point` as WKB `PointZ`                            |
| `CityObjects.{id}.geographicalExtent`     | `bbox` (unioned with the extent computed from the object's subtree geometry; reconstructed from `bbox` on export) |
| `appearance.materials`                    | `materials.parquet`                                         |
| `appearance.textures`                     | `textures.parquet`                                          |
| `appearance.vertices-texture`             | inlined into `texture_lod*` UV pairs                        |
| `geometry-templates.templates`            | `geometry_templates.parquet`, one row per template          |
| `geometry-templates.vertices-templates`   | encoded into the template WKB geometry                      |
| `metadata`                                | `city.other` and/or the [STAC Item](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/metadata)'s `city3d:*` fields |
| `transform`                               | applied to the geometry at encode; not a structural key — MAY be carried informationally in `city.other` |
| `extensions`                              | the [`city.extensions` metadata key](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/metadata) + [extension-derived columns](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/extensions) |
| other object members                      | the object-table `other` column, restored into `attributes` on export (JSON; null when the object has none) |

chapters.title: Worked example
chapters.description: A CityGML CM record encoded as CityParquet, end to end, with the CityJSON form alongside.
chapters.body:
This constructed example walks a single small feature from the **CityGML conceptual
model** into CityParquet end to end, then shows the same feature as CityJSON so the
mapping from that serialisation is visible too. It is **illustrative** — coordinates
and ids are abbreviated, though every step follows the encoding rules of the
specification body. For **real records** read from an actual file, see the embedded
examples on the [Geometry, LoD & spatial metadata](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/geometry-semantics)
and [Object table schema](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/object-table-schema) pages.

The feature: a `Building` with one `BuildingPart`; the part has an LoD 2.2 `Solid`
whose two boundary surfaces are a `RoofSurface` and a `WallSurface`; the building
carries one core attribute (`yearOfConstruction`) and one ADE attribute (`height`); the
roof surface has a material.

## As CityGML CM → CityParquet

In the CM the two features map to two object rows; the boundary surfaces become the
solid's per-face semantics; the attribute values become typed columns; the material
becomes a per-face reference into the material sidecar.

**Object table `building.parquet` (two rows):**

| id | feature_id | object_type | parents | children | bbox | geometry_lod2_2 | geometry_properties_lod2_2 | material_lod2_2 | ex_height | yearOfConstruction |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `b-42` | `b-42` | `Building` | — | `[b-42-0]` | *(union of children)* | *null* | *null* | *null* | `12.5` | `1998` |
| `b-42-0` | `b-42` | `BuildingPart` | `[b-42]` | — | `{xmin…zmax}` | *WKB PolyhedralSurfaceZ (2 faces)* | `{type:"Solid", surfaces:[…], face_semantics:[0,1], shells:[[2]]}` | `{"":{"values":[3,3]}}` | *null* | *null* |

**Notes.**

- The root `Building` has `feature_id == id` (`b-42`), and its child `BuildingPart`
  inherits it, so both rows of the family share `feature_id = b-42`.
- The `Building`'s attributes sit on its own row; a CM feature's own thematic
  attributes stay with the feature. `yearOfConstruction` was inferred `BIGINT`; the ADE
  attribute `height` became the `ex_height` column.
- The `Solid`'s two boundary surfaces were flattened into a 2-face
  `PolyhedralSurfaceZ`; the roof/wall semantics live in the
  `geometry_properties_lod2_2` struct, face-aligned (`face_semantics: [0, 1]`), with
  `shells: [[2]]` recording the single solid's single shell the WKB flattened away.
- The LoD `2.2` is carried by the column suffix alone — `geometry_properties_lod2_2`
  has no `lod` field.
- Material is **per face**: the two faces both reference material `3`, so
  `material_lod2_2` is `{"":{"values":[3,3]}}`. The `3` is the **`id`** of a row in
  [`materials.parquet`](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/appearance-templates), not a row position.
- The `Building` carries no geometry of its own, so its
  [`bbox`](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/geometry-semantics) is the union of its part's.

**`materials.parquet` — the referenced row:**

| id | name | diffuseColor | … |
|---|---|---|---|
| `3` | `roofmat` | `[0.9, 0.1, 0.1]` | … |

## The same feature as CityJSON

CityJSON is one serialisation of that CM feature, and the
[CityJSON mapping](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/mapping-cityjson) governs its fields. The source
below encodes exactly the feature above; comparing it with the table shows what the
encoding changes.

```jsonc
{ "type": "CityJSONFeature", "id": "b-42",
  "CityObjects": {
    "b-42":   { "type": "Building", "children": ["b-42-0"],
                "attributes": { "yearOfConstruction": 1998, "+height": 12.5 } },
    "b-42-0": { "type": "BuildingPart", "parents": ["b-42"],
                "geometry": [ { "type": "Solid", "lod": "2.2",
                  "boundaries": [ [ [[0,1,2,3]], [[4,5,6,7]] ] ],
                  "semantics": { "surfaces": [ {"type":"RoofSurface"}, {"type":"WallSurface"} ],
                                 "values": [ [0, 1] ] },
                  "material": { "": { "values": [ [3, 3] ] } } } ] } },
  "vertices": [ /* … */ ] }
```

What the encoding changes, relative to this serialisation:

- `+height` → the `ex_height` column (a leading `+` cannot be a portable column name).
- The nested `boundaries` are resolved against `vertices` (and the feature's
  `transform`, not shown) into world-coordinate WKB; the source quantisation is not
  retained.
- The per-shell `semantics.values` (`[[0, 1]]`) is flattened to the per-face
  `face_semantics` (`[0, 1]`), and the shell partition it carried moves to
  `shells: [[2]]`.
- The per-shell `material.values` (`[[3, 3]]`) is flattened to the per-face
  `[3, 3]`, and the feature-local material index becomes the sidecar `id`.

chapters.title: Specification & file format
chapters.description: The normative CityParquet data model — columns, geometry encoding, metadata, and mapping rules.
chapters.body:
**Draft specification**

CityParquet is at version **0.1.0-draft**. Some normative column shapes are still
affected by unresolved design questions (see [Open questions](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/open-questions)), so
parts of this specification MAY change.

CityParquet is a columnar encoding of the **CityGML conceptual model** in Apache
Parquet. It stores 3D city model data in a cloud-native layout that can be queried
efficiently from object storage — filtering by feature type, attribute, level of
detail (LoD), bounding box, and 3D geometry — while preserving the semantics needed
to reconstruct or exchange the source model.

Every table is a standard Parquet file, readable by any Parquet reader. Where the
geometry allows, CityParquet also conforms to **GeoParquet**, so a city model's
footprints open in ordinary GIS tooling; the [metadata](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/metadata) page
defines exactly where that reach ends.

CityParquet is **not** a rendering or streaming format, and does not itself define a
tiling scheme.

This specification is the *what*. The *why* behind each choice — the alternatives
considered and the trade-offs accepted — lives in the companion
[design decisions](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/design-decisions), linked inline throughout. Open items are
collected in the [open questions](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/open-questions), and each unresolved point in the
body links there with a 🟡 marker.

## Requirement levels

The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT**, and **MAY** are to
be interpreted as described in RFC 2119 / RFC 8174 when, and only when, they appear in
capitals.

Sections are marked *(normative)* or *(informative)*; unmarked sections default to
normative.

## Type notation

Column types are written in DuckDB/Arrow logical-type notation: `VARCHAR`, `BIGINT`,
`DOUBLE`, `BOOLEAN`, `BLOB`, `JSON`, `LIST<T>`, `STRUCT<…>`. Their physical Parquet
encoding is:

| Logical type | Physical Parquet encoding |
|---|---|
| `VARCHAR` | `BYTE_ARRAY` (UTF8) |
| `BIGINT` | `INT64` |
| `DOUBLE` | `DOUBLE` |
| `BOOLEAN` | `BOOLEAN` |
| `DATE` | `INT32` with the `DATE` logical type |
| `TIME` | `INT64` with the `TIME` logical type (microseconds, UTC-normalised) |
| `TIMESTAMP` | `INT64` with the `TIMESTAMP` logical type (microseconds, UTC-normalised) |
| `BLOB` | `BYTE_ARRAY` (no logical type) |
| `JSON` | `BYTE_ARRAY` (UTF8), tagged with the Arrow field-metadata extension `ARROW:extension:name = arrow.json`. A reader without Arrow extension support sees a UTF8 string. |
| `LIST<T>` | Parquet `LIST` of nullable items |
| `STRUCT<…>` | Parquet group (see the individual column for field types and nullability) |

A column **MAY** additionally be dictionary-encoded. That is a writer's choice and
changes nothing about the logical type; where it is particularly worthwhile —
`object_type`, the appearance enumerations — this specification says so, but never
requires it.

## The pages

    Files, roles, versioning, and the by-module object-table layout.
    Reserved columns, typed attribute columns, and addresses.
    WKB encoding, surface semantics, the per-LoD columns, and `bbox`.
    Materials, textures, and geometry templates.
    Parquet key-value metadata, the STAC Item, and GeoParquet `geo` / CRS.
    CityGML ADEs, CityJSON Extensions, and the escape hatch.
    The converter reference.
    A record, end to end.

chapters.title: A · Table & schema strategy
chapters.description: One object per row in per-module wide tables, with typed attribute columns.

sections.heading: One city object per row, in per-module wide tables
Typed attribute columns, not EAV or a JSON blob
Addresses stored as a struct attribute, not a separate table

chapters.body:
How CityParquet lays out city objects into tables and columns: one object per row, split into per-module wide tables, with attributes stored as typed columns rather than an entity–attribute–value store, and addresses kept inline as a struct. The prior art weighed here is chiefly 3DCityDB's relational model.

## One city object per row, in per-module wide tables

decided

**Decision.** Each CityObject is one row in a wide table, and the dataset is **split into one table per CityGML module** (`building.parquet`, `transportation.parquet`, …; every type in a module shares the module's file — see [the file package](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/design-decisions/files-crs-metadata)). Every table has reserved structural columns (`id`, `object_type`, `parents`, `children`, `bbox`, `geometry_lod*`, …) plus typed attribute columns. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/object-table-schema) → *Reserved columns*.

**Alternatives considered.**

- (a) a **single wide table** holding every object type, one object per row;
- (b) **multi-table decomposition** (object + property + geometry tables), the **3DCityDB v5** relational shape;
- (c) **per-module wide tables** — one file per CityGML 3.0 module, one object per row — chosen (file mechanics in the file package decision).

**Why this.** The target workload is analytical queries read *directly from cloud object storage*. Multi-table normalisation (b) forces **joins on read**, and joins are expensive over HTTP range requests — each join side is a separate scan and fetch. A single all-types table (a) keeps the single scan but mixes heterogeneous object types into one very **sparse** schema (a Building and a Road share few attributes): storage stays cheap — Parquet's run-length/dictionary encoding makes the NULLs nearly free — but predicate/projection pushdown gains little, because a scan still spans every type. Splitting by **module** (c) keeps the single-scan property *per module* and makes each file's column statistics tight, so a query over buildings scans only `building.parquet`. The module is the partition **native to the CityGML CM** CityParquet encodes, and it keeps closely-related peers together — the four Transportation types all specialise `AbstractTransportationSpace` and share most attributes, so folding them into `transportation.parquet` costs little sparsity while sparing the reader four fragmented files. This also suits **hive partitioning**: a reader prunes whole files from their footer statistics — skipping most files without reading their data — and touches only the ones a query needs. 3DCityDB normalises because in a relational database the tables sit on one disk, where a join is cheap and normalisation is good practice; CityParquet targets columnar files read over object storage, where a join means separate scans and range requests, so it keeps an object's data together in one row.

**Trade-off.** Splitting by module means a reader must know which module holds which type, and a cross-module query touches several files rather than one. A query for one leaf type (say roads) scans its whole module file (also railways, waterways, squares), recovering most of the lost selectivity through the `object_type` predicate and row-group statistics. We accept this to buy fast, well-pruned per-module queries with a single uniform rule. To be *measured*, not asserted, in the paper.

**Status.** Decided; the per-module split is the layout the specification defines.

## Typed attribute columns, not EAV or a JSON blob

decided

**Decision.** Each attribute is stored as its own typed Parquet column (`BIGINT`/`DOUBLE`/`VARCHAR`/`BOOLEAN`/`DATE`…) — not an entity–attribute–value store, and not a single JSON blob. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/object-table-schema) → *Attribute types and promotion*.

**Alternatives considered.**

- (a) one JSON blob column holding all attributes;
- (b) a **3DCityDB-style EAV** property table with `val_int`/`val_double`/`val_string`/… columns, one property per row;
- (c) one typed column per attribute — chosen.

**Why this.** The main reason is **predicate and projection pushdown**, and the simplicity of querying over the network: per-attribute typed columns let an engine prune row groups on an attribute predicate and read only the columns a query projects. They also compress far better than the alternatives. An EAV property table is flexible to store — any attribute fits without a schema change — but it pushes that complexity onto every read: reassembling an object means self-joins or pivots, queries grow awkward, and performance suffers. A single JSON blob is opaque to the engine, so it offers no pushdown at all. This is why we do not follow 3DCityDB's `val_int`/`val_double`/… EAV multiplexing.

**Trade-off.** We must handle schema/type inference and rely on consistent attribute names. When the same attribute name has inconsistent types across objects we promote (int→double) or fall back to `VARCHAR`/`JSON` — a small, bounded loss of fidelity, though the inconsistency is a property of the source data that any encoding must confront. We must also track which columns are dynamic attributes; these are recorded in the `attributes` metadata key (every other column is a reserved structural column).

**Status.** Decided and implemented. Union types are a possible future refinement.

## Addresses stored as a struct attribute, not a separate table

decided

**Decision.** An address is a reserved `address` column on the object table — a `LIST<STRUCT<…>>`, since an object may have several — not a separate address table. The struct holds a **lean subset of 3DCityDB v5's `ADDRESS` table**: the structured postal fields (`street`, `house_number`, `po_box`, `zip_code`, `city`, `state`, `country`), a `free_text` unstructured fallback, and a `location` holding WKB `MultiPointZ`. 3DCityDB's bookkeeping columns (the id, the cross-system identifier pair, the original-payload `content`/`content_mime_type`) and a JSON escape hatch are deliberately **not** carried. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/object-table-schema) → *Addresses*.

**Alternatives considered.** 3DCityDB v5 keeps a dedicated address table with a foreign key to the property table. For the struct itself: invent a field set, adopt 3DCityDB's in full, or adopt a lean subset of it.

**Why this.** A separate address table reintroduces a join-on-read for what is simply a property of the city object; keeping it inline preserves the single-scan property of the one-object-per-row layout above. Basing the fields on 3DCityDB's postal columns means the two models line up where it matters, because 3DCityDB is where most CityGML addresses in practice already live. The bookkeeping and escape-hatch columns were dropped to keep the struct small and queryable — an address is postal data plus a point, and `free_text` absorbs anything unstructured.

`location` is a **WKB `MultiPointZ`**, not a boundary. CityJSON's `address[].location` is a `MultiPoint` whose `boundaries` index the source vertex list, which CityParquet resolves and discards — a preserved index would dangle. A coordinate does not, so storing geometry here is what makes addresses round-trip at all.

**Trade-off.** The lean field set cannot capture a source address member outside the postal fields, and there is no per-address escape hatch, so such members are dropped (a documented round-trip loss). Accepted: the structured fields plus `free_text` cover the practical cases, and the alternative — carrying every 3DCityDB column plus a JSON blob — bloats the struct for data city models rarely populate.

**Status.** Decided, including the struct schema.

chapters.title: B · Geometry encoding
chapters.description: WKB geometry, parallel property columns, one geometry column per LoD, and encode-time transform.

sections.heading: WKB geometry (including 3D), not native geometry or EWKB
Non-WKB geometry information lives in parallel columns
transform applied at encode time, not a structural key

chapters.body:
How CityParquet stores geometry: as WKB blobs for interoperability today, with everything WKB cannot carry pushed into parallel JSON columns, one geometry column per level of detail, and CityJSON's quantised vertices expanded to world-coordinate doubles at encode time. Prior art weighed here: GeoParquet, Apache Iceberg, PostGIS EWKB, GeoArrow, and 3DCityDB.

## WKB geometry (including 3D), not native geometry or EWKB

open

**Decision.** Geometry is stored as WKB `BLOB` in the dataset CRS. 3D solids → `PolyhedralSurfaceZ`; multi/composite solids → `GeometryCollectionZ`; surfaces → `MultiPolygonZ`. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/geometry-semantics) → *Geometry encoding*.

**Alternatives considered.**

- (a) **WKB blob** — the OGC Simple Features encoding; interoperable but opaque to the columnar engine. Used by **GeoParquet** and **Apache Iceberg** for their geometry columns.
- (b) **PostGIS EWKB** — WKB plus a per-record SRID (see [the CRS decision](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/design-decisions/files-crs-metadata) for the CRS angle).
- (c) **native Parquet `GEOMETRY`** — the GeoParquet 2.0 direction (vectorisable, coordinate-level pushdown).
- (d) **custom Arrow / GeoArrow** packed-coordinate extension type (typed, zero-copy).

**Why this.** **Interoperability today.** WKB opens unmodified in DuckDB-spatial, GDAL, QGIS, and PostGIS; it is the common denominator that GeoParquet and Iceberg both settled on. The native `GEOMETRY` logical type is the more "correct" columnar direction and is adopted where it applies (see Status below), but it inherits the same limit: its **3D** vocabulary reaches `GeometryCollection` and no further, so the solid geometry that is CityParquet's whole point falls outside it. We follow 3DCityDB's precedent of using WKB even for 3D.

**Trade-off.** WKB is opaque to the columnar engine — parsed on every access, poorer compression, no coordinate-level predicate pushdown. Concrete tooling limit found in practice: **DuckDB-spatial cannot decode our multi-surface/solid WKB**. That limit is itself a reportable finding (columnar-3D tooling is immature). Many libraries advertise WKB support but only for 2D simple features.

**Status.** WKB is decided, and option (c) is adopted alongside it: the native Parquet `GEOMETRY` logical type annotates the same WKB bytes rather than replacing them, so a column is simultaneously a plain `BYTE_ARRAY` and a GeoParquet 2.0 geometry column.

The annotation is **not** applied to every geometry column. It is applied exactly where `geo` declares the column — the [declaration rule](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/metadata) — because a solid column's `PolyhedralSurface Z` is outside the geometry model of the engines that consume the annotation. DuckDB promotes any annotated column and converts it eagerly, and its `GEOMETRY` type has no `PolyhedralSurface`, so annotating one costs the ability to read it at all rather than buying anything. What CityParquet's most distinctive columns gain from GeoParquet 2.0 is therefore nothing; what its footprint columns gain is native typing and a per-chunk bounding box with `zmin`/`zmax`. That asymmetry is a fact about the ecosystem's 3D support, not a choice this format makes, and it is the same asymmetry the WKB-versus-native decision above already turns on.

**Why not (d).** The main goal behind a native Arrow geometry type is native statistics and not needing a separate `bbox` column — and the Parquet `GEOMETRY` logical type with `GeospatialStatistics` delivers exactly that, over WKB bytes every existing reader already understands. That leaves a packed or indexed Arrow encoding offering only a modest size advantage over WKB, which does not justify a second encoding to specify, write, read and test across three implementations. GeoParquet 2.0 reaches the same conclusion, permitting `"WKB"` alone and dropping the GeoArrow native encodings 1.1.0 allowed.

An index-based layout would also have to go a level deeper than GeoArrow's own native geometry types support, to carry CityParquet's shell/solid nesting — so the interoperability argument for reusing a community encoding does not hold here either.

## Non-WKB geometry information lives in parallel columns

decided

**Decision.** A `geometry_properties_lod*` **`STRUCT`** column (per LoD) holds what WKB cannot: the geometry type, the semantic-surface definitions (`surfaces`), the surface→face mapping, and the solid shell structure. The fixed-shape parts are typed struct fields (`type`, `face_semantics LIST<INT>`, `shells LIST<LIST<INT>>`); only `surfaces` — heterogeneous per surface — stays `JSON`. Appearance goes in separate `material_lod*` / `texture_lod*` columns (see [appearance and shared resources](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/design-decisions/appearance-shared-resources)). Crucially, the surface→face mapping is stored **flattened and aligned to WKB face order** — a flat `face_semantics` array where `face_semantics[i]` is the surface index of WKB face `i` — rather than as a nested per-shell tree (the shape CityJSON's `values` uses). See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/geometry-semantics) → *Geometry properties and semantics*.

**Alternatives considered.**

- (a) copy CityJSON's nested `semantics.values` verbatim (simplest, faithful, but analysis-hostile — a nested tree keyed by shell/surface that must be walked and index-resolved);
- (b) **3DCityDB's** `geometry_properties`: a flat hierarchy descriptor keyed by `geometryIndex` into the polyhedral surface — but it carries *only* geometric hierarchy, **not** semantic surface types/attributes (3DCityDB keeps those as separate features);
- (c) the flattened, face-aligned form — chosen: 3DCityDB's flat index-into-the-polyhedral-surface idea, but keeping the CityGML CM's semantic surface definitions inline.

**Why this.** WKB / OGC Simple Features has **no slot** for the CityGML CM's semantic surfaces (WallSurface/RoofSurface…), materials, textures, LoD, or template references — once geometry is a blob these must live somewhere explicit. And for the *analytical* target workload, the mapping must be cheap to use: with `face_semantics` aligned to WKB faces, "the roof faces of this solid" is a positional filter and per-surface attributes are one dereference into `surfaces`, instead of a nested-tree traversal. Verbatim CityJSON `values` would force procedural JSON walking on every surface-level query.

**Trade-off.** Semantics live *beside* geometry rather than inside it (the consumer zips the two columns by face index); and aligning `face_semantics` to the *emitted* faces means a strict 1:1 with the source's surfaces is not guaranteed where faces are dropped (a future consideration, noted under open questions).

**Status.** Decided and implemented. A native `LIST<INT>` `face_semantics` column and a strict-1:1 guarantee are [future work](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/open-questions).

## One geometry column per LoD

decided

**Decision.** Each LoD gets its own `geometry_lod*` + `geometry_properties_lod*` column pair, and every geometry column is LoD-suffixed — there is no un-suffixed `geometry` column, and a suffix always carries a minor version (`geometry_lod1_0`, never `geometry_lod1`). The primary geometry column is *declared* in metadata rather than identified by name. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/geometry-semantics) → *Levels of detail*.

**Alternatives considered.**

- (a) **one column per LoD** (`geometry_lod1_0`, `geometry_lod2_2`, …) — chosen;
- (b) **one long column, one row per LoD** (extra `lod` column);
- (c) **one file per LoD** (`cityobjects_lod1.parquet`, …).

**Why this.** A query wanting only LoD2 reads only the LoD2 column (projection pushdown) and never touches the LoD1 bytes — the columnar win. The expected access pattern is "the same LoD across many objects" or "several LoDs of one object", not "different objects each at a different LoD", so option (b) would sacrifice pruning for a case we do not expect. Option (b) also breaks **attribute encoding**: with one row per LoD, either every attribute is **duplicated** across an object's per-LoD rows, or only the highest-LoD row carries them — neither works well. Option (c) makes the reader resolve which file holds which LoD.

**Trade-off.** Wider schema as the LoD count grows; each LoD needs its matching `geometry_properties_lod*`. Uniform suffixes cost a small canonicalisation of the LoD *string* — a source LoD of `1` names the column `geometry_lod1_0` and exports as `1.0` — but the LoD *value* is unaffected, and the suffix is the single source of truth (no redundant `lod` value is stored).

**Status.** Decided and implemented. Column-per-LoD is the normative layout; the row-per-LoD and file-per-LoD alternatives are rejected.

## transform applied at encode time, not a structural key

decided

**Decision.** CityJSON's quantised integer vertices and `transform` (scale + translate) are applied during encoding; coordinates are stored as world-coordinate doubles. The source `transform` is **not** a structural metadata key — re-quantisation on decode is the decoder's choice, with parameters it selects. A producer MAY still carry the source `transform` (and other source-dependent header fields) informationally in the catch-all `other` metadata key. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/geometry-semantics) → *Geometry encoding*.

**Alternatives considered.** Preserve the quantised integers + `transform` (better compression, byte-exact round-trip) vs expand to doubles and discard the transform (simpler analysis representation).

**Why this.** A world-coordinate double representation is the simplest thing for analytical consumers and for feeding WKB to GIS tooling — no client needs to know the quantisation scheme. Quantisation is fundamentally a *decoding* concern: a consumer that wants compact integer output picks a `transform` suited to its own precision/extent needs, so reproducing the source's transform buys nothing that the decoder can't choose better itself.

**Trade-off.** We lose the exact original quantisation, so a strict byte-level round-trip of vertices is not offered; model-level round-trip (identity, hierarchy, attributes, semantics, appearance, templates) is unaffected.

**Status.** Decided — transform applied at encode; not a structural key, but MAY be carried informationally in `other`.

chapters.title: C · Spatial access
chapters.description: A bbox struct column with optional Hilbert ordering for pruning.

sections.heading: bbox STRUCT column + optional Hilbert ordering

chapters.body:
How CityParquet makes spatial window queries prune cheaply over object storage: a typed 3D `bbox` struct column that feeds Parquet's per-row-group statistics, with optional Hilbert-curve ordering to tighten them. The prior art weighed here is 3DCityDB's `envelope` column and GeoParquet's `bbox` struct.

## bbox STRUCT column + optional Hilbert ordering

decided

**Decision.** Every row carries a 3D `bbox` STRUCT `[xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax]` in the geometry CRS. Rows may optionally be written in Hilbert-curve order on the bbox centroid. A parent without its own geometry gets the **union** of its descendants' bboxes; bbox is null only when nothing in the subtree has geometry. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/geometry-semantics) → *Spatial metadata*.

**Alternatives considered.**

- **3DCityDB** carries an `envelope` column on the feature table for spatial indexing;
- **GeoParquet** carries a `bbox` struct column (2D `[xmin,ymin,xmax,ymax]` or 3D) matching the geometry CRS — the model we follow, extended to 3D.

**Why this.** A typed `bbox` column feeds Parquet's per-row-group **min/max statistics**, which is how a spatial window query prunes row groups over object storage *without downloading the file*. Hilbert ordering clusters spatially-near rows into the same row group, tightening those per-group bboxes so pruning is more selective. Null bboxes were shown **not** to corrupt min/max statistics, so pruning stays sound.

**Trade-off.** One `bbox` per row must cover everything the row stores — every LoD, and every descendant — so it is a **union**, and therefore looser than a per-geometry box would be. A loose box costs false-positive reads; a tight one drawn from a single LoD would wrongly prune rows whose other LoDs extend beyond it, which is the error that actually loses data. Hilbert ordering costs a sort at write time.

**Status.** Decided. Null-bbox soundness — that null bboxes do not corrupt the row-group min/max statistics — is confirmed; the pruning selectivity and window-query gains from Hilbert ordering are to be measured and reported in the paper.

chapters.title: D · Appearance & shared resources
chapters.description: Geometry separated from appearance; shared resources in deduplicated sidecars.

sections.heading: Geometry separated from appearance; shared resources in deduplicated sidecars
Geometry templates in a sidecar, instances via a template struct

chapters.body:
How CityParquet handles resources shared across many objects: materials and textures are separated from geometry and deduplicated into sidecar files referenced by global id, and reusable geometry templates live in their own sidecar with instances carrying only a small `template` struct. Prior art weighed here: 3DCityDB's appearance table and CityJSON's shared appearance/geometry-template pools, following the OBJ / COLLADA / glTF principle of separating geometry from appearance.

## Geometry separated from appearance; shared resources in deduplicated sidecars

decided

**Decision.** `materials.parquet` and `textures.parquet` hold reusable definitions; the object table's nullable `material_lod*`/`texture_lod*` JSON columns reference them by the sidecar's **dataset-global `id`** — matched against the `id` column, never a row position. Texture UV coordinates are **inlined** into the object table's texture map. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/appearance-templates) → *Appearance encoding*.

**Alternatives considered.**

- **3DCityDB** keeps a separate appearance table with a foreign key to the feature table;
- **CityJSON** keeps an `appearance` object with a shared material/texture pool referenced by feature-local indices.

**Why this.** Follows the recurring project principle — geometry and appearance should be *separable*, as in OBJ / COLLADA / glTF. Materials and textures are referenced by *many* objects, so storing them once and referencing beats duplicating them per object; global dedup (by canonical JSON) is the columnar analogue of CityJSON's shared appearance pool. Two normalisations were needed relative to the source: references become **dataset-global** sidecar `id` values (not CityJSONSeq's feature-local indices), and UV indices are replaced inline by the actual `[u, v]` pairs so the object table is self-contained.

**Trade-off.** Resolving appearance needs a sidecar lookup; because indices are global, the exporter must re-intern feature-local pools (and re-derive UV indices into a `vertices-texture` pool) on the way back to CityJSON.

**Status.** Decided and implemented; a sidecar definition file is written exactly when the source has definitions to put in it. The global-id + inline-UV normalisation was settled during implementation.

## Geometry templates in a sidecar, instances via a template struct

decided

**Decision.** Reusable templates live in `geometry_templates.parquet`, using the same geometry strategy as the object table — including the per-LoD column grammar: `geometry_lod*` + nullable `geometry_properties_lod*` / `material_lod*` / `texture_lod*`. An instancing object stores a `template` STRUCT `{id, point (WKB PointZ), transformationMatrix (LIST<DOUBLE>, a flat 16-element row-major 4×4)}` in the object table. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/appearance-templates) → *geometry_templates.parquet*.

**Alternatives considered.** Inline the template geometry at each instance (simple, but defeats the whole point of an implicit/instanced geometry) vs reference a shared template (chosen).

**Why this.** Implicit geometries exist precisely to share one geometry across many instances; a sidecar of templates referenced by id preserves that compaction. Template vertices are in **local** coordinates and are **not** subject to any dataset-level transform, so template WKB stores raw doubles. The sidecar follows the per-LoD column grammar so that one LoD-naming rule holds across the whole format, rather than making this the sole place where an LoD rides in a value.

**Trade-off.** Resolving an instance needs a sidecar lookup plus applying its `transformationMatrix` and reference `point`. A template is one geometry at one LoD, so the per-LoD columns leave each row sparse — accepted as the price of the uniform naming rule.

**Status.** Decided and implemented; 🟡 an object instantiating *several* templates remains an [open question](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/open-questions), since `template` is a single struct.

chapters.title: E · Files, CRS & metadata
chapters.description: The core + sidecar file package, CRS once per file, and dataset metadata.

sections.heading: Core + sidecar file package; by-module split
CRS once per file, not per record
Dataset metadata: a `city` object mirroring GeoParquet's `geo`

chapters.body:
How a CityParquet dataset is packaged on disk: a directory with a self-contained core table plus optional sidecars, split by CityGML module, the CRS stored once per file rather than per record, and dataset metadata written to both the Parquet footer and a package-level `metadata.json` STAC Item. Prior art weighed here: the shapefile package, PostGIS EWKB, and GeoParquet's metadata conventions.

## Core + sidecar file package; by-module split

decided

**Decision.** A dataset is a *directory* of per-module object tables plus optional sidecars — one file per **CityGML 3.0 module**, never a single combined table. Every type in a module shares the module's file, distinguished by the `object_type` column; a `BuildingPart` is a Building-module row, the four Transportation types all live in `transportation.parquet`. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/dataset-package) → *Dataset package layout*.

**Alternatives considered.** A single monolithic file vs a multi-file package; splitting by individual object type (`road`, `railway`, … each their own file) vs splitting by module.

**Why this.** The guiding analogy is the **shapefile**: the core file is usable for analysis on its own, even without the sidecars (like using a `.shp` without its `.prj`). Splitting by module gives schema clarity and narrower scans; the module is the CM's own thematic partition, and it keeps a feature family (a Building with its parts, the transportation types) in one file, preserving locality for hierarchy traversal. A finer split — one file per individual object type — would instead fragment those closely-related families across files and inflate the file count for little gain.

**Trade-off.** A shared file mixes several types; consumers filter on `object_type` to separate them, and a single-leaf-type query scans its whole module file.

**Status.** Decided; the by-module split is the layout the specification defines, delivering the per-module pruning argued in [the schema strategy](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/design-decisions/schema-strategy).

## CRS once per file, not per record

decided

**Decision.** The CRS is stored once per file as **PROJJSON** in Parquet metadata (GeoParquet convention), not as a per-record SRID. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/metadata) → *Metadata*.

**Alternatives considered.** **PostGIS EWKB** embeds an SRID per geometry record (allowing a different CRS per row); **GeoParquet** deliberately uses one CRS per column and defaults to WGS84 if unspecified.

**Why this.** City models share a single CRS per file, so a per-record SRID is redundant overhead. It also matters for statistics: Parquet keeps column statistics at the column level, and a different CRS per row would make per-row-group min/max meaningless — undermining the very pruning that [spatial access](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/design-decisions/spatial-access) relies on. GeoParquet reached the same conclusion.

**Trade-off.** Merging datasets in mixed CRSs requires reprojection to a common CRS first; there is no per-row CRS escape hatch. Revisit only if mixed-CRS merges become a real requirement.

**Status.** Decided and implemented.

## Dataset metadata: a `city` object mirroring GeoParquet's `geo`

decided

**Decision.** Dataset-level metadata (version, provenance, CRS, the geometry-column registry, the `attributes` list, extensions, and an `other` catch-all for arbitrary fields such as the source `transform` and the source's own header metadata) is written to Parquet footer key-value metadata under a single **`city`** object — deliberately shaped like GeoParquet's `geo` object (`version`, `primary_column`, `columns`, …). A GeoParquet-conformant `geo` object is written *alongside* it for interop, and a package-level `metadata.json` STAC Item mirrors it for discovery. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/metadata) → *Metadata*.

**Alternatives considered.** A flat set of scalar footer keys vs one structured `city` object. Putting **all** geometry-column metadata into GeoParquet's `geo` object was also considered and rejected: declaring a solid column there can make the whole file unreadable to GeoParquet tools (see the [declaration rule](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/metadata)).

**Why this.** One `city` object that mirrors `geo` is legible to anyone who knows GeoParquet, keeps the `cityparquet:` namespace off individual keys, and gives solid columns a home (`city.columns`) that `geo` cannot provide.

**Trade-off.** The legal columns are described twice — in `city.columns` and in `geo.columns` — which must be kept consistent; accepted, because the alternative (one object) breaks solid-bearing files for GeoParquet readers.

**Status.** Decided.

chapters.title: F · Extensions
chapters.description: CityGML ADEs and CityJSON Extensions, typed where possible, escape-hatched otherwise.

sections.heading: Extensions: typed where possible, escape-hatched otherwise

chapters.body:
How CityParquet carries extensions to the CityGML conceptual model — a CityGML **ADE**, or the equivalent **CityJSON Extension**: four extension mechanisms map to four encodings, promoting extension data to typed columns where Parquet allows it and falling back to JSON values where it does not.

## Extensions: typed where possible, escape-hatched otherwise

decided

**Decision.** Four extension mechanisms, four encodings. See the [specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification/extensions).

- **Extended feature types** → grouped by module like core types: an extension with its own module gets a file named after that module (`Energy` ADE → `energy.parquet`), while a type specialising an existing class joins that class's module file. The CityJSON `+` marker is stripped from file names.
- **Extended semantic surfaces** → keep their source name, including CityJSON's `+` prefix, *inside* the `geometry_properties_lod*` JSON value (they are not promoted to column names).
- **Extended attributes** (`+height`) → the leading `+` is replaced with `ex_`, giving column `ex_height`.

The extension declaration itself is referenced via the `extensions` Parquet metadata key.

**Alternatives considered.** Keeping all extension data in the `other` JSON escape hatch vs promoting extension attributes to first-class typed columns. For file names: preserving CityJSON's `+` marker (`+foo.parquet`), transliterating it to a prefix (`ext_foo.parquet`), or dropping it.

**Why this.** Extension attributes benefit from the same typed-column advantages as [core attributes](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/design-decisions/schema-strategy), so they are promoted — but Parquet column names cannot carry a leading `+`, hence the `ex_` convention. Extended *semantics* live in JSON values, where `+` is legal, so no renaming is needed there. The `+` is dropped from file names because it is a CityJSON *encoding* marker — it exists to keep extension types from colliding with core types inside a JSON document — and has no meaning in the CM this format encodes, nor any business in a file name.

**Trade-off.** The `ex_` rename accepts a low, bounded risk of colliding with a genuine `ex_`-prefixed attribute. Dropping the `+` from file names accepts a similar bounded risk: an extension type whose name matches a core type would want the same file. Representing CityGML ADE namespaces beyond this convention is not yet solved.

**Status.** Conventions decided and implemented; the CityGML ADE namespace / object-class metadata representation is **open** — see the [Open questions](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/open-questions).

chapters.title: Design decisions
chapters.description: The decisions behind CityParquet, each with the alternatives considered and the trade-off accepted.
chapters.body:
This section records **why** CityParquet is designed the way it is. The
[Specification](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/specification) records _what_ the format is; where the two
overlap, the specification is authoritative on the _what_ and this section
explains the _reasoning_. Prior art weighed throughout: PostGIS, GeoParquet,
Apache Iceberg, and 3DCityDB.

## How to read a decision

Each decision follows the same shape:

- **Decision** — the one-line resolution.
- **Alternatives considered** — the options weighed, so the choice is positioned.
- **Why this** — the reasoning that selected it.
- **Trade-off** — the cost knowingly accepted.
- **Status** — decided or open.

Open items link to [Open questions](https://cityparquet.open3d.city/open-questions).

    One object per row; typed attribute columns; addresses.
    WKB geometry, parallel property columns, one column per LoD, encode-time transform.
    The bbox column and Hilbert ordering.
    Geometry/appearance separation and shared-resource sidecars.
    The file package, one CRS per file, dataset metadata.
    How ADEs and CityJSON Extensions are encoded.
